newsitem.title: USA: Global bankers eye Japan resolve in Nomura scandal.
newsitem.headline: Global bankers eye Japan resolve in Nomura scandal.

text.p: Foreign bankers view recent troubles at Nomura Securities Co Ltd as a sign of more pervasive Japanese financial woes and are intently scrutinizing Japan's handling of the scandal.
Nomura officials and banking sources in major financial centers around the world said the scandal's direct market impact should be largely limited to Japan.

But a failure of Japanese regulatory bodies to send a harsh message to Nomura could have global implications, sapping confidence in Japan's corruption-fighting resolve and damaging faith in its private financial firms over the long run.
"People here in the U.S. are definitely looking at how Japanese policymakers handle a problem like this," said Allen Sinai, chief global economist at Primark Decision Economics and the WEFA Group.

"The troubles of a Nomura and other financial institutions are dealt with by the institutions themselves in a very, very slow fashion. The problems are institutional, which delays the day of awakening for Japan," Sinai added, noting he expects more troubles for Japanese banks and securities houses.

Nomura's troubles surfaced on March 6 when Japan's biggest brokerage publicly admitted that two of its executives had funneled undue profits to a real estate company linked to a "sokaiya" corporate racketeer through illicit stock transactions.

Just last week prosecutors and securities regulators raided Nomura's headquarters and other locations for evidence in the case, leading Nomura's chairman and president Masashi Suzuki to publicly concede that the company's business would suffer.

Already, pension funds, bond issuers, Japanese municipalities, insurance companies and Nippon Telegraph and Telephone, the nation's largest telecommunications company, have pulled business from Nomura.
And on Friday, Japan's electric power firms -- major issuers of domestic straight bonds -- said they may drop Nomura from their future underwriting syndicates.

The latest problems are not the first for Nomura, which was sanctioned along with the subsidiaries of three other Japanese broker-dealers by the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission in the early 1990s during Japan's loan loss guarantee scandal.
Paul Gerlach, associate director at the SEC'S enforcement division, said that at that time the problems discovered were not as serious as those found in Japan.
This time around, the immediate international fallout for Nomura, which has a significant presence in the U.S. and Europe, also appears limited.
A spokesman for Nomura Securities International in New York refused to comment on the scandal, calling it a "Tokyo problem."
But Brian Fitzgibbon, senior vice president at Nomura Capital Management in New York, said clients had been briefed on the problems at the parent company and were sticking by the firm.
Nomura representatives in London echoed a similar refrain and bankers said the raids in Japan were unlikely to have an immediate impact on its position in Europe, which is chiefly in fixed income.
"The scandal is more a domestic concern, and it is very much on the equity side," a banker familiar with Nomura said. "It is unlikely to affect international fixed income business, for now."
But bankers throughout the world's major financial centers did sound a note of caution. They said Nomura's latest problems exemplified a wider malaise among Japanese securities houses.
Japanese authorities must send a clear signal that unethical financial practices will be severely punished in order to restore a modicum of international confidence, they noted.

"The demonstrated lack of business ethics and level playing field and plain dealing reveals an arrogant almost criminal (business) culture," said a Hong Kong-based fund manager, noting that his firm's business relationships with Japanese houses were characterized by "misunderstandings and miscommunications."

"It is just a deep-rooted behavior (pattern) up there that is really preventing them from obtaining what should be theirs -- and that's the control and guidance of East Asian capital flows," he added.
The fund manager said he believed Nomura viewed itself as "untouchable" and "not answerable to authorities."
Depending on the findings of Japan's regulatory watchdog, the SESC, the finance ministry could revoke Nomura's business licenses or order it to halt some or all business for up to six months.
Should the deals be found to have violated the commercial code's ban on payoffs to racketeers, legal action could also be initiated.
But market sources in Tokyo said Japanese authorities are unlikely to punish Nomura in a way that would risk choking off the huge liquidity the brokerage provides to capital markets.

The sources expect the Ministry of Finance, depending on the findings of an investigation by the SESC, to order Nomura to halt some or all of its business for up to six months. This would be a stiff punishment that would take a bite out of Nomura's profits and prestige but would not threaten the stability of the markets.

Traders say that while Nomura has the biggest market share in stockbroking, its influence on the share market is less significant than in bonds, making a temporary absence from the market less damaging overall.
